## Observations

1. Since every term is positive, every adjacent ratio is defined. The sequence is geometric exactly when all adjacent ratios equal the first ratio, \(A_2/A_1\).
2. For each \(i\) from \(3\) through \(N\), the equality \(A_i/A_{i-1}=A_2/A_1\) is equivalent to \(A_iA_1=A_{i-1}A_2\). This comparison uses exact integer arithmetic, even when the ratio is fractional.
3. When \(N=2\), there is only one adjacent ratio, so the sequence is always geometric.
4. Each comparison needs only the first two terms, the immediately preceding term, and the current term.

## Solution sketch

1. > Since every term is positive, every adjacent ratio is defined. The sequence is geometric exactly when all adjacent ratios equal the first ratio, \(A_2/A_1\).

   Read \(N\) and the sequence from standard input. Use the first two terms as the reference pair without evaluating their quotient.

2. > For each \(i\) from \(3\) through \(N\), the equality \(A_i/A_{i-1}=A_2/A_1\) is equivalent to \(A_iA_1=A_{i-1}A_2\). This comparison uses exact integer arithmetic, even when the ratio is fractional.

   Scan from the third term onward and compare the two cross-products at each position. At the first mismatch, print `No` and stop.

3. > When \(N=2\), there is only one adjacent ratio, so the sequence is always geometric.

   If the scan finishes without a mismatch, print `Yes`. For \(N=2\), the scan is empty, so the same rule gives the correct answer without a special case.

4. > Each comparison needs only the first two terms, the immediately preceding term, and the current term.

   Process one adjacent pair at a time without building a list of ratios or products. The algorithm takes \(O(N)\) time and \(O(1)\) auxiliary space beyond the input sequence.
